Verify endpoint coverage against Apollo's public API documentation before building

approval.cost: No fee or cost is stated anywhere in the OAuth documentation
approval.trigger: Registration approval itself is the gate: 'To set up an OAuth flow, you need to provide Apollo with details about the purpose of your organization using the flow. Once registration is approved, you can use the Apollo playground to test the OAuth flow before attempting to implement it.' The approval sits in front of testing and implementation, not just public distribution. No dev-mode user cap is documented; the documented pre-approval restriction is that the playground (and thus flow testing) is unavailable until registration is approved. The OAuth documentation describes no marketplace or directory listing process for partner apps.
approval.wait: Not stated (no approval duration, SLA, or rejection process in the docs)

blockers.detail: Unlike most providers, you cannot build or test first and seek approval later: registration (with details about the purpose of your organization using the flow) must be approved before the Playground, and thus flow testing, is available. The docs state no timeline for that approval.
blockers.howToClear: Submit the registration early and design the rest of your integration while waiting; there is no documented fast path.
blockers.title: Approval before you can even test

blockers.detail: 'To authorize your integration via OAuth, an Apollo end user must have the necessary permissions.' On plans with custom permission profiles, the user needs the 'Can authorize third-party apps/integrations via OAuth' permission; on other plans, the user must hold the Admin or Billing and Seat Manager permission profile. A user without it is redirected with status_code=403 and an error message appended to your redirect URL.
blockers.howToClear: Handle the 403 error case on your callback explicitly and tell users up front which permission they need.
blockers.title: Per-user authorizer permission gate

blockers.detail: 'In the future, if you edit these scopes, you need to repeat this entire authorization flow to set up OAuth again.' Combined with refresh rules (on refresh you may only reduce scopes, and only to scopes originally defined at registration), the registered scope set is a launch decision.
blockers.howToClear: Get the scope set right at registration; include read_user_profile explicitly in any scope parameter you pass.
blockers.title: Scope edits restart the whole setup

alternatives: API keys (sent in the x-api-key header; endpoint-scoped or a 'master key' with access to every endpoint; a key acts on YOUR Apollo account, so it is a first-party auth method, not a delegated per-user consent flow)
flavor.recommended: A partner OAuth app registration using the authorization code grant (the only grant type Apollo documents: 'Apollo supports the OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant type')
flavor.why: The object is an OAuth app registration for partners, created inside Apollo under Settings > Integrations > API Keys > OAuth registration. Registration generates a client ID and client secret. Users sign in to Apollo, see your app name, logo, and requested scopes, approve, and are redirected back with a code you exchange for access + refresh tokens.

humanMust: Register the app in the Apollo UI and wait for registration approval before testing
Copy the client secret at generation ('The only time the secret is displayed is when it is generated. Store it in a secure location as it will not be shown again')
Confirm endpoint coverage and that your users hold the authorizer permission (see Blockers)
name: Apollo
nuances: Refresh-token rotation revokes the old pair: 'Once you use the refresh token to generate a new access and refresh token, the existing tokens are automatically revoked and are no longer valid.' Persist the replacement pair atomically.

Scope parameter traps: if you pass scope in the authorization URL and need read_user_profile, you must include it explicitly in that parameter; if scope is omitted, the registration scopes are used. Apollo adds read_user_profile and app_scopes by default at registration.
Redirect URL limits: must use https; maximum 4 redirect URLs (comma-separated).
Endpoint coverage ceiling: 'This authorization method supports only the API endpoints listed in Apollo's public API documentation.' Verify your use case is covered before building.

Access tokens live 30 days (expires_in 2592000); identify the token owner via GET app.apollo.io/api/v1/users/api_profile. The developer Playground (OAuth Integration > Playground) is the documented manual test path after approval.
prerequisites: An Apollo account able to open Settings > Integrations > API Keys
App Name, App Logo, OAuth Redirect URL (https; up to 4, comma-separated), and Scopes
Details about the purpose of your organization using the flow (part of registration)

steps.detail: 'This authorization method supports only the API endpoints listed in Apollo's public API documentation.' Also confirm your users can authorize: on custom-permission plans they need the 'Can authorize third-party apps/integrations via OAuth' permission; otherwise the Admin or Billing and Seat Manager profile.
steps.title: Confirm endpoint coverage and authorizer permissions

steps.detail: Settings > Integrations > API Keys > OAuth registration. Enter App Name, App Logo, OAuth Redirect URL (must use https; up to 4, comma-separated), and Scopes ('Only add scopes that are necessary'; Apollo adds read_user_profile and app_scopes by default). The registration includes details about the purpose of your organization using the flow. Click Submit, then wait for approval.
steps.title: Register the app (approval required)

steps.detail: 'The only time the secret is displayed is when it is generated. Store it in a secure location as it will not be shown again.'
steps.title: Copy the client ID and client secret

steps.detail: OAuth Integration > Playground: enter a redirect URL, 'Get authorization code', paste code + client secret, 'Get access token', 'Fetch data'. Only available once registration is approved.
steps.title: (Optional) Test in the Playground

steps.detail: app.apollo.io/#/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&response_type=code&scope=...&state=... response_type must be code; scope and state are optional (omitted scope = registration scopes). The user reviews the permissions and grants access; handle the status_code=403 permission-error redirect on your callback.
steps.title: Build the authorization URL

steps.detail: POST app.apollo.io/api/v1/oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code, code, client_id, client_secret, optional redirect_uri. Response: access_token, refresh_token, token_type Bearer, expires_in 2592000 (30 days), scope. Call the API with the access token as a bearer token. Refresh at the same endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token; the old token pair is revoked on use, and refresh scopes may only be reduced.
steps.title: Exchange the code; call the API; refresh

tagline: Textbook authorization code flow behind an unusual gate: Apollo must approve your app registration, with no stated timeline, before you can even open the Playground to test it. After that, the traps are a per-user authorizer permission and scope edits that restart the whole setup.

time.active: ~30 min of registration + ~half a day of flow code
time.total: Unknown: registration approval duration is not stated
